narrative:
The model estimated a 59.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning failure was judged slightly more likely than passing. That estimate led to your application being denied; it is not a certainty, but it was high enough to create concern about your readiness for bar success.

The strongest factor pushing toward failure was your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, which is slightly below the 3.23 average among accepted students. The next most influential factor was your first-year class rank decile of 5, below the accepted-student average of 6, which also pushed the prediction toward failure. Your third-year decile of 7 was above the accepted average of 5.79 and was the main factor pushing in the opposite direction, toward passing, but it did not outweigh the first two concerns. Your LSAT score of 37 was close to the accepted average of 37.18 and was not among the top three drivers.

To improve your position, focus on strengthening your academic readiness before reapplying. Meet with an admissions or academic advisor, ask what evidence would address the first-year and GPA concerns, and consider additional coursework or a structured bar-prep readiness plan. A reapplication should show improved preparation and a realistic plan for bar success.
